title: Use of Force Case Law Update: May 4 to 9, 2026
description: Two published Fourth Circuit decisions this week are the cleanest teaching pair since Barnes v. Felix came down a year ago. In both, the court denied qualified immunity to an officer who shot a retreating suspect, and in both the anchor was Tennessee v. Garner. Ruffin v. Davis, filed April 29, involved an armed 17-year-old who ran from a Columbia, South Carolina officer during a COVID curfew and was shot as he looked back; a gun on a fleeing suspect, by itself, is not an immediate threat. Byers v. Painter, filed in late April, involved a man in mental health crisis holding a hatchet at his waist and walking away on his parents' property; deadly force against that retreating subject was not justified, over a dissent. On April 27 the Supreme Court denied certiorari in Barnes v. Felix for the second time, leaving Deputy Constable Felix's qualified immunity final. The three cases show the totality framework cutting both ways.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: May 11 to 16, 2026
description: A corrective week after a spring of Supreme Court decisions that broadened merits review and narrowed qualified immunity. In Manning v. City of Tulsa, a published Tenth Circuit opinion filed March 30, the court denied qualified immunity to former Tulsa officer Betty Shelby in the September 2016 shooting of Terrence Crutcher, holding that Tennessee v. Garner, a Supreme Court deadly force decision squarely on point, put the unlawfulness of shooting an unarmed, non-dangerous subject beyond debate without any further specificity. The case now goes to a jury. On April 27 the Supreme Court denied certiorari a second time in Barnes v. Felix, ending that case with the officer winning under the totality framework the Court itself announced a year earlier. And on April 9 the Colorado Court of Appeals held that Boulder could not charge more than $8,000 for body camera footage of a fatal officer-involved shooting. Nothing from the Ninth Circuit and nothing from California in this episode.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: August 3 to 8, 2026
description: Two items this week, and they share one fault line. In Smith v. Olvera, decided July 14, a divided Ninth Circuit panel granted qualified immunity to an Elko, Nevada officer who struck a prone, just-crashed suspect in the head with a baton in the dark. The majority ruled only that no earlier case put the officer on notice; it did not say the head strikes were lawful. Judge Thomas dissented, writing that whether the man was taking furtive or threatening actions or was simply lying there incapacitated was a jury question. On June 22, the Supreme Court declined to hear the City of Los Angeles's appeal in the McBride case, leaving in place a six to five en banc ruling that a jury could find the last two shots, fired after a knife-wielding man had fallen, were excessive. Both cases turn on the moment a threat may have ended and force continued.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: August 31 to September 5, 2026
description: No federal circuit, state high court, or United States Supreme Court decision on law enforcement use of force came down in the past seven days, and the Supreme Court is in summer recess until the first Monday in October. This week covers four 2026 decisions not previously reviewed. The Eleventh Circuit in Edwards v. Grubbs let stand $21 million against an Atlanta officer personally for a dart-mode Taser deployment, without warning, on a fleeing man above a steep embankment. The Fifth Circuit in Searles v. City of Houston and the Ninth Circuit in Foer v. City of Seattle granted qualified immunity on the clearly established prong only, leaving the merits of two fatal shootings undecided. A divided Fourth Circuit panel in Harold v. Hagan vacated immunity for a canine release on a prone, compliant burglary suspect, though a rehearing petition was pending. Across all four, the warning and the documented opportunity to comply is the fact courts reach for first.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: September 26 to October 3, 2026
description: Edwards v. Brown on pepper spray decontamination and grievance tolling, Mason v. Talley on restraint to a fixed object, Hyttinen v. Frantti on warrant entry, Fambrough v. City of East Cleveland on orders from the top, and Andrade v. Collier County Sheriff. The October 4 follow-up sweep of the circuits, the Supreme Court order lists, and the California Court of Appeal is folded into the written brief for this week.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: October 5 to 11, 2026
description: Navejas v. City of El Paso on a single Taser deployment against a 70-year-old man with dementia, Fischer v. Phillips on shooting into a slow-moving car, Byrum v. Knox County on jail medical response, and the Supreme Court's denial in Shelby v. Manning.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: October 12 to 18, 2026
description: Vision Bank v. Avery and Burke v. Pitts on deadly force and hostile motion, Rockett v. Eighmy on locking children in holding cells, Martinez v. Hidalgo County, Bailey v. Michigan Department of Corrections, and Estate of Stinson v. Streicher.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: October 19 to 25, 2026
description: Astorga v. Villanueva on supervisor liability for crowd control, Kilnapp v. City of Cleveland on an officer shot by her partner, Bond v. Sheriff of Ottawa County and a $33 million jail death verdict, Garcia v. United States on a hostage killed in a rescue, and two published California search decisions.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: October 26 to November 1, 2026
description: United States v. Zamora on when a seizure starts, Collazo v. Otsego County on control holds at a shots-fired call, Merrill v. Seagraves on a second Taser cycle, People v. Ball, People v. Steele, People v. Hicks on prone restraint, and Turner v. Sims on supervision language.

title: Use of Force Case Law Update: November 2 to 7, 2026
description: Johnson v. Adgar: a 40mm foam baton round fired indiscriminately into a retreating San Jose protest crowd was excessive force, but the officer gets qualified immunity, and the Ninth Circuit sends a Bane Act question to the California Supreme Court. Read with Astorga v. Villanueva from the October 25 episode.
